A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-reward image-editing work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching across the revised layout.

before.justification: v1 reports original Real-Edit and MagicBrush experiments, human evaluations, component ablations and qualitative results in Tables 1–6 and accompanying figures.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 7–11, failure cases and repeated GPT-4o evaluation results.

M1.justification: The reward-score/text encoding, attention-based conditioning, additive U-Net conditioning, diffusion objective and inference conditions remain the same. Section 4.2 now specifies one transformer block and distinguishes the two linear projections; these clarify previously underspecified implementation details without establishing a changed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use InsPix2Pix-derived RewardEdit-20K, Real-Edit and MagicBrush for the same instruction-based editing task. The new challenging-sample analysis selects 500 low-scoring examples from existing RewardEdit-20K; it changes sampling and analysis within retained coverage rather than introducing another dataset, domain or task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same comparison methods, and the new CLIP/FID comparison in Table 7 reuses Table 1's method roster. Additional appendix controls vary existing baseline settings or compare against original dataset targets. DPO-Diffusion and Pony Diffusion are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds CLIP/FID evaluation, a data-matched training control, selection of 500 samples scoring at most 2, individual-reward training and a 512-versus-256 resolution experiment with batch size maintained through gradient accumulation. The evaluation prompt also changes from integer scores in v1 Figure 14 to floating-point scores in v2 Figure 16. Whether retained results were rerun with that prompt is unspecified.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained reward-format, integration and inference-score ablations, v2 tests whether improvements persist with matched editing data, how individual reward perspectives contribute, performance on difficult training examples and sensitivity to training resolution. Appendix A and Figure 10 additionally analyze object-count and spatial-position failures.

E5.justification: Appendix D.3 newly reports five GPT-4o evaluation tests, with accuracy fluctuations within 1% and score fluctuations within 0.05. v1 provides no corresponding repeat-count or variability information. This concerns evaluator stability, not repeated model-training runs or confidence intervals for the main results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 and the original qualitative results remain unchanged, but Tables 7–11 add substantial findings. Table 8 reports following/preserving/quality scores of 2.90/2.88/3.52 for the data-matched baseline versus 3.39/3.43/3.80 for the reward model. Other additions report difficult-example improvements, individual-reward tradeoffs, lower scores at 512 training resolution and explicit count/spatial failures.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives and conditioning equations retain their substance. Equation numbering and the Linear1/Linear2 notation clarify presentation; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no new formal derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: RewardEdit-20K, multi-reward conditioning, Real-Edit and improved editing with InsPix2Pix and SmartEdit. Additional appendix evidence supports these existing claims without materially changing their scope.

C2.justification: v2 newly acknowledges that maximum reward conditions do not guarantee maximum-quality outputs and identifies quantifier/spatial-understanding failures. Appendices C–D discuss limitations of CLIP/FID, restricted training-data provenance, GPT-4o versus human annotation, resolution-experiment constraints and reward text as corrective information. Section 6.3 also adds a tentative explanation for lower human scores.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code/dataset release; v2 provides a reported code-release link without establishing dataset availability. v2 also specifies GPT-4o version 2024-08-06, one reward-encoder block, projection roles, separate MRC training for each model and gradient accumulation for the resolution experiment. Most original implementation settings remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Pony Diffusion discussion, references including SEED-Data-Edit and Ctrl-U, and removes several earlier references, including RLAIF and the human-feedback language-model training paper. Appendix D.4 adds a substantive comparison with DPO-Diffusion concerning feedback granularity, multiple perspectives and training stability. The central positioning around noisy editing supervision remains intact.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the seven-section narrative are retained, with localized clarifications and citation-style changes. New appendix sections precede the original material, which moves from A–C to E–G. There are also new cross-reference errors, including Section 6.3 pointing to Table 11 instead of the retained human-evaluation Table 3.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to a single-column format, substantially resizing and repositioning figures, tables and equations. v2 adds failure-case and dataset-example Figures 10–11 and Tables 7–11. Original appendix Figures 10–14 are retained as Figures 12–16 rather than removed.

improvement.justification: The strongest gain is better support for the central reward-conditioning claim: Table 8 adds an explicit data-matched control addressing whether improvements merely reflect additional editing data. Individual-reward ablations, alternative metrics, evaluator-repeatability information and concrete failure analysis substantially strengthen validation and transparency. The unchanged headline results gain supporting evidence. Unexplained evaluation-prompt provenance and erroneous cross-references remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive improvements.
